title: Anatomy, Thorax, Heart Left Anterior Descending (LAD) Artery -- Introduction
content: The heart is a muscular pump that provides the force necessary to circulate blood throughout the body. Cardiac muscle requires blood flow to function. This flow is provided by the coronary arteries. The right coronary artery arises from the right aortic sinus of the aorta, just above the aortic valve. Similarly, the left coronary artery, or the left main coronary artery, arises from the left aortic sinus. The left main coronary artery divides into the left anterior descending artery, which supplies the anteroseptal wall of the heart, and the circumflex coronary artery, which supplies the posterior and lateral portions. See Image. Anatomy of the Heart.

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Heart Left Anterior Descending (LAD) Artery -- Structure and Function
content: The LAD carries almost 50% of the blood carried by the coronary circulation. During systole, the heart muscle squeezes over the perforating arteriolar branches and causes a complete cessation of flow. Therefore, coronary flow occurs during diastole when the pressure from the cardiac contraction does not obstruct the blood flow. Therefore, the coronary flow is dependent on diastolic blood pressure. Like any other capillary bed, the coronary circulation is controlled by local autoregulation mediated by demand-dependent arteriolar dilatation. [1] [2]

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Heart Left Anterior Descending (LAD) Artery -- Structure and Function -- Structure
content: The coronary arteries run on the epicardial surface of the heart to avoid being compressed by the cardiac muscle when it contracts. The left anterior descending artery (LAD) is the largest coronary artery that runs anterior to the interventricular septum in the anterior interventricular groove, extending from the base of the heart to the apex. The LAD gives 2 sets of branches. The septal branches perforate the interventricular septum to supply the anterior two-thirds of the septum. These are numbered S1 and S2, onwards starting from the base to the apex. The second set of branches course over the anterior aspect of the left ventricle and are called diagonal branches. These are also numbered D1 and D2, onwards starting from proximal to distal. Around the apex, the LAD anastomoses with the terminal branches of the posterior descending artery, usually a branch of the right coronary artery.

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Heart Left Anterior Descending (LAD) Artery -- Structure and Function -- Structure
content: Depending upon the length of the LAD, the LAD is classified into 4 types: type-I – does not supply the left ventricular apex, type-2 – supplies part of the apex, the rest is supplied by the right coronary, type3 – supplies the entire apex, and type-4 – supplies the apex and >25% of the inferior wall (wrap around). A small left conus branch usually arises from the proximal LAD and anastomoses with its counterpart from the right coronary artery around the aortic conus and also with the vasa vasorum of the aorta and the pulmonary artery. Usually, a couple of small right ventricular branches also arise from the LAD, supplying small parts of the anterior right ventricle.

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Heart Left Anterior Descending (LAD) Artery -- Structure and Function -- Structure
content: Multiple anastomoses exist between the coronary arteries. The terminal LAD anastomosis with the terminal branches of the posterior descending artery (PDA) in the posterior interventricular groove about 90% of the time. In 10% of the cases, no such anastomoses exist. Within the interventricular septum, septal branches of the LAD freely anastomose with the septal branches of the PDA. However, the flow in all of these anastomoses is small and does not suffice in case of sudden occlusion of a parent vessel. If the parent vessel occludes slowly, often the anastomoses can gradually enlarge to provide meaningful flow. The LAD and its branches are epicardial and give off “end-arteries,” arterioles that perforate the myocardium to supply it.

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Heart Left Anterior Descending (LAD) Artery -- Embryology
content: The origin of the coronary arteries is not entirely clear. Coronary arteries may arise from the epicardial layer or the sub-epicardial vessel plexus.

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Heart Left Anterior Descending (LAD) Artery -- Blood Supply and Lymphatics
content: Vasa Vasorum are tiny blood vessels supplying blood to the coronary vessels. The heart's lymphatics drain back along the coronary arteries, emerge from the fibrous pericardium along with the aorta and the pulmonary trunk, and empty into the trachea-bronchial lymph nodes and mediastinal lymph trunks.

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Heart Left Anterior Descending (LAD) Artery -- Nerves
content: Sympathetic fibers from the cardiac plexus innervate the coronary arteries. The left coronary plexus arises mainly from the left half of the deep part of the cardiac plexus and accompanies the left coronary artery branches to supply the left atrium and ventricle.

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Heart Left Anterior Descending (LAD) Artery -- Physiologic Variants
content: Myocardial Bridging: Although coronary vessels run over the epicardial surface of the heart, sometimes the artery courses intra-myocardially under a muscle “bridge.”  Bridging is found in 0.5% to 40% of individuals when identified clinically and 15-85% in autopsy studies. [3]

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Heart Left Anterior Descending (LAD) Artery -- Physiologic Variants
content: Absent Left Main: In some cases, the left main coronary artery is absent, and the LAD and the circumflex arteries arise from a single cloacal opening. In other cases, these 2 arteries arise from separate openings directly from the aorta.

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Heart Left Anterior Descending (LAD) Artery -- Physiologic Variants
content: Coronary Fistulae: Coronary fistulae are rare in adults but account for 50% of pediatric coronary anomalies. A fistula between a coronary artery and the cardiac cavity is called a coronary-chimeral fistula , and that between a coronary artery and vein is called an arterio-venous fistula . Most fistulae are congenital. Acquired ones are usually iatrogenic or traumatic.

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Heart Left Anterior Descending (LAD) Artery -- Physiologic Variants
content: Anomalous Origin: Anomalous origin of the left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery is a rare malformation (incidence of 0.25–0.50%) in children with abnormal cardiac development, leading to a mortality rate of 90% in unoperated infants. [4]

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Heart Left Anterior Descending (LAD) Artery -- Surgical Considerations
content: Given the importance of the LAD for coronary blood flow, surgeons often try to bypass it with the best possible graft during coronary artery bypass surgery, usually using the left internal mammary artery (LIMA). LIMA is mobilized from the chest wall during such surgery, keeping its origin intact. Side branches are tied off, and the end is anastomosed to the LAD. LIMA-to-LAD grafts are very durable.

title: Anatomy, Thorax, Heart Left Anterior Descending (LAD) Artery -- Clinical Significance
content: The LAD is the largest coronary artery. Atherosclerosis or thrombotic occlusion of this vessel causes myocardial infarction involving large areas of the heart muscle's anterior, septal, and apical portions, leading to serious impairment of cardiac performance. For the same reason, it is important to restore the flow in the LAD during revascularization by percutaneous or surgical methods. [5] [6] Infarcts involving LAD occlusion frequently involve the apex. This can be accompanied by the formation of clots in the apex. These clots can embolize and cause stroke or systemic embolism.
